extra.message:
Stored XSS via safe_break filter bypassing HTML auto-escaping — Authenticated attacker injects arbitrary JavaScript that executes in other users' browsers, enabling session theft, credential phishing, data exfiltration of PII/financial data, and CSRF-style actions against all viewers of the affected escalation, organization, or deal pages. [verified: The safe_break filter at crm/templatetags/crm_extras.py:176 calls mark_safe() on user-supplied text after only replacing newlines with
— zero HTML escaping anywhere in the chain (no model validators, no form clean_* methods, no view sanitization, no CSP headers). Customer contacts can inject arbitrary JavaScript into comment bodies via EscalationCommentForm, which then executes in staff/admin]

Stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via safe_break Filter on User Content — Session hijacking (despite HttpOnly cookies, XSS can perform actions as the victim via fetch/XHR with CSRF tokens), credential phishing via fake login forms injected into the CRM, data exfiltration of all visible CRM data, privilege escalation by performing admin actions as a stolen staff/admin session. [verified: Same root cause as finding 0: safe_break applies mark_safe() to user-controlled fields (customer_summary, internal_summary, comment body, org notes, deal notes) with no HTML sanitization at any layer. A malicious staff member can inject XSS in customer_summary that executes in customer browsers via the portal, and a customer contact can inject XSS in comment replies that executes in staff browsers]

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) via Jinja2 Template with user-controlled fragment — Remote code execution on the server via Jinja2 SSTI. An attacker can execute arbitrary Python code, read sensitive files including environment variables and database credentials, access the Django SECRET_KEY, modify the database, and gain full control of the application server. [verified: Same as finding [1]/[16]: user-controlled 'fragment' embedded directly into Jinja2 Template string enabling server-side code execution.]

Arbitrary file write via path traversal in user-controlled name — An attacker can write arbitrary content to the filesystem, potentially overwriting application code, creating malicious files (web shells, crontab entries, SSH authorized_keys), modifying settings, or corrupting the database. This can lead to code execution and full system compromise. [verified: Same as finding [5]/[19]: unsanitized 'name' param with body content written to traversable path enabling arbitrary file write.]

Command injection via user-controlled host in os.system ping — Remote code execution on the server with the privileges of the Django process. An attacker can read sensitive files (database credentials, SECRET_KEY, source code), modify or delete data, establish reverse shells, and potentially escalate to full system compromise. [verified: Same as finding [0]/[17]: user-controlled 'host' concatenated into os.system() shell command without any sanitization or escaping.]

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) via Jinja2 Template with user-controlled fragment — Remote code execution on the server, full application compromise, access to SECRET_KEY, database credentials, and all stored data. [verified: User-controlled 'fragment' GET parameter (line ~134) is concatenated into a Jinja2 Template string and rendered; no input sanitization or sandboxing exists, enabling arbitrary Python code execution.]

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) via Jinja2 in Partner Console — Remote code execution on the server, full system compromise, access to SECRET_KEY, database credentials, and all customer data. [verified: Same as finding [1]: user-controlled 'fragment' concatenated into Jinja2 Template and rendered with no sanitization, enabling server-side code execution.]

Jinja2 Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) in partner console — Remote code execution on the application server, full system compromise [verified: Same as finding [1]/[16]/[26]: user-controlled fragment embedded in Jinja2 Template with no sandboxing, enabling arbitrary server-side code execution.]

Arbitrary File Write via user-controlled name and request body — Write arbitrary files anywhere the Django process has write access, enabling webshell deployment, configuration overwrite, Python module injection for code execution, and data destruction. [verified: 'name' GET param (line ~143) used unsanitized in path construction and request.body written to the resolved path; path traversal enables writing arbitrary content anywhere the process has write access.]

OS Command Injection via user-controlled host in os.system ping — Remote code execution on the server with the privileges of the Django process, enabling data theft, credential exfiltration, lateral movement, and full system compromise. [verified: User-controlled 'host' GET parameter (line ~151) is concatenated directly into os.system('ping -c 1 ' + host) with zero sanitization; _wrk_gate is an access gate, not an input-sanitizing control.]

Hardcoded default Django SECRET_KEY in settings.py — If the application is deployed without setting the DJANGO_SECRET_KEY environment variable, all cryptographic operations use a publicly known secret. An attacker can forge session cookies to impersonate any user (including platform admins), bypass CSRF protection, craft valid password reset tokens to take over accounts, and reduce the security of API key hashing. [verified: Same hardcoded SECRET_KEY fallback on line 16-17 as findings 0/2; the known default exists in source control and .env.example with no enforcement mechanism to require a real key in production, enabling full authentication bypass.]

Hardcoded Django SECRET_KEY Fallback in Settings — Session forgery allowing impersonation of any user including platform admins, CSRF token forgery bypassing CSRF protection, password reset token forgery enabling account takeover, API key hash bypass if the pepper is known. [verified: Same hardcoded SECRET_KEY fallback on line 17 as finding 0; the known default 'dev-secret-change-me-please-not-for-production' is in source control with no guard preventing production use, enabling cryptographic forgery of sessions, CSRF tokens, and password reset tokens.]

Missing rate limiting / brute-force protection on login endpoint — An attacker can brute-force user passwords by submitting unlimited authentication attempts. Since email addresses are the username and are often publicly known or guessable, this enables credential stuffing and password guessing attacks against all user accounts including platform admins. [verified: MinimumLengthValidator enforces password complexity but not attempt frequency; AppLoginView.form_valid/invalid (accounts/views.py:35-70) record attempts but never block after N failures, and no rate-limiting library or custom throttle exists anywhere in the project.]

Missing Rate Limiting / Brute-Force Protection on Login — Attackers can perform unlimited credential guessing / brute-force attacks against user accounts, potentially compromising weak passwords and gaining unauthorized access to the CRM and all its data. [verified: LoginEvent.recent_failures() is defined at accounts/models.py:134 but is never called by AppLoginView.form_invalid() (accounts/views.py:58) or any middleware; no django-axes, django-ratelimit, or custom throttle exists in requirements.txt or MIDDLEWARE, leaving /accounts/login/ with zero brute-force protection.]

SSRF via HTTP redirect following in webhook test delivery (ENABLE_REAL_WEBHOOK_DELIVERY=True) — When real webhook delivery is enabled, an attacker who can create webhooks (staff with can_manage_organization permission) can configure a webhook pointing to an attacker-controlled server that issues a 302 redirect to internal services (cloud metadata, local admin interfaces, databases). The Django server will follow the redirect and fetch the internal resource, potentially exfiltrating cloud cre [verified: urllib.request.urlopen in test_delivery follows redirects by default with no HTTPRedirectHandler override. WebhookForm.clean_target_url() validates the initial URL against private IPs but cannot prevent a malicious target from redirecting (302) to internal addresses like 169.254.169.254. When ENABLE_REAL_WEBHOOK_DELIVERY=True, authenticated staff with can_manage_organization can exploit this SSRF,]

Path Traversal via user-controlled packet_ref in file path construction — Arbitrary file read from the server filesystem, exposing source code, configuration files with database credentials, SECRET_KEY, environment variables, and uploaded documents from other tenants. [verified: 'packet_ref' GET param (line ~40) joined directly to BASE_EXPORT_DIR via / operator with no path sanitization; traversal sequences like ../../etc/passwd escape the intended directory and read arbitrary files.]

Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) via user-controlled URL in partner console — An attacker can make the server initiate HTTP requests to internal network resources, including cloud metadata services (AWS/GCP/Azure IMDS), internal admin interfaces, databases, other microservices, and localhost services. This can lead to information disclosure, authentication bypass, and pivoting within the internal network. [verified: Same as finding [4]: user-controlled URL passed to urllib.urlopen() with no validation, enabling internal service probing and cloud metadata access.]

Sensitive data (SSN and credit card numbers) written to disk in plaintext — Sensitive personally identifiable information (SSN and credit card numbers) is stored in plaintext JSON files on the server filesystem. If the server is compromised or the files are exposed through other vulnerabilities (path traversal, misconfigured serving), this data could be accessed by attackers. This also violates PCI-DSS and data protection regulations. [verified: Same as finding [7]: plaintext SSN and credit card data written to disk at user-controlled path with no encryption or access controls.]

Sensitive PII (SSN/credit card) written to plaintext file on disk — Persistent storage of unencrypted SSNs and credit card numbers on the filesystem, creating a high-value target for exfiltration via path traversal, backup compromise, or other filesystem access vulnerabilities. [verified: SSN and credit card numbers from GET params written as plaintext JSON to disk at a user-controlled path (lines ~90-96); no encryption, creating a persistent sensitive-data store.]

Path traversal and sensitive data written to disk via user-controlled path in partner console — Arbitrary file write of PII/PCI data to uncontrolled locations, potential disk fill, overwrite of critical files [verified: Same as finding [7]/[32]: user-controlled ref path with traversal enables writing sensitive PII (SSN/card) as plaintext JSON to arbitrary filesystem locations.]

XML External Entity (XXE) injection via lxml parser with entity resolution enabled — An attacker can read arbitrary local files on the server, perform SSRF requests to internal network services, cause denial of service via billion laughs attack, and potentially achieve remote code execution in certain configurations. [verified: Same as finding [2]/[20]: lxml parser with DTD loading and entity resolution enabled on user-supplied XML, enabling XXE file read and SSRF.]

Privilege escalation via client-controlled cookie/header in partner console — Unauthorized access to elevated functionality by setting a cookie or header client-side [verified: Same as finding [12]: client-controlled ops_badge cookie/header determines privilege level with no server-side verification or cryptographic signing.]

XML External Entity (XXE) Injection in Partner Console — Read arbitrary local files, perform SSRF to internal services, denial of service via billion laughs attack, exfiltrate sensitive data. [verified: Same as finding [2]: lxml parser with DTD/entity resolution enabled parsing user-controlled XML body, enabling file read and SSRF via external entities.]

XML External Entity (XXE) Injection in partner console — Arbitrary file read on the server, internal network SSRF, potential denial of service [verified: Same as finding [2]/[20]/[31]: lxml parser with DTD/entity resolution on user XML body enables XXE-based file read and internal SSRF.]

DEBUG mode enabled by default in Django settings — In production deployments where DJANGO_DEBUG is not explicitly set to False, detailed error pages expose sensitive configuration including SECRET_KEY, database credentials, file paths, and application internals to any user who triggers an error. This dramatically amplifies the impact of other vulnerabilities and aids in reconnaissance. [verified: Same DEBUG=True default on line 17-18 as findings 1/3; without DJANGO_DEBUG explicitly set False, error pages leak sensitive configuration and the conditional security hardening at line 124 is never applied.]

DEBUG=True as default configuration enabling verbose error pages — Exposure of source code, SECRET_KEY, database credentials, environment variables, and internal application state to unauthenticated users via Django debug error pages. Also disables all production security hardening (HSTS, secure cookies, SSL redirect). [verified: DEBUG defaults to True via _env_bool('DJANGO_DEBUG', default=True) on line 18; when unset in production, verbose error pages expose SECRET_KEY, DB credentials, and internal state, and the 'if not DEBUG' block on line 124 leaves secure cookies/HSTS/SSL redirect disabled.]

DEBUG Mode Enabled by Default with Information Disclosure — Exposure of SECRET_KEY, database credentials, and other secrets in error pages; detailed stack traces revealing internal application logic and file paths; missing secure cookie flags leading to session hijacking over HTTP; potential for Django debug toolbar access exposing SQL queries and configuration. [verified: Same DEBUG=True default on line 18 as finding 1; unset DJANGO_DEBUG in production enables detailed error tracebacks leaking secrets (SECRET_KEY, DB password) and disables the security hardening gated by 'if not DEBUG' on line 124.]

Deal stage transition bypass via create/edit forms — Authenticated staff users can bypass the deal pipeline state machine to arbitrarily jump deals between stages (e.g., lead → closed_won, closed_lost → qualified), manipulating pipeline metrics, financial reporting, and deal workflow enforcement. [verified: DealForm.Meta.fields includes 'stage' (crm/forms.py:80) and both create_deal (crm/views/deals.py:69-78) and edit_deal (line 117-118) save the form without calling is_valid_deal_transition(), while the dedicated change_stage view (line 146-159) does validate transitions. Any authenticated staff with can_manage_organization access can POST an arbitrary valid stage choice through create or edit, bypa]

Open redirect via user-controlled lane parameter in partner console — An attacker can craft URLs that redirect users to malicious websites, enabling phishing attacks, credential theft, and token/session exfiltration. Since the redirect originates from the trusted application domain, users are more likely to follow it. [verified: Same as finding [6]/[21]: unsanitized 'lane' param passed to redirect() enabling open redirect phishing attacks.]

Business Logic Flaw — arbitrary ledger state and balance manipulation — Manipulation of financial ledger balances by supplying negative amounts, unauthorized state transitions, and corruption of business-critical financial data. [verified: User-supplied 'amount' (can be negative, inflating balance) and 'state' applied directly to ledger dict (lines ~66-69) with no validation, authorization checks, or integrity verification.]

Mass assignment / parameter pollution via unchecked dict.update with user JSON in partner console — An attacker can override security-sensitive fields like role, tier, approved, and balance by supplying matching keys in the JSON payload. This can lead to privilege escalation (changing role from 'viewer' to potentially higher), bypassing approval checks, and manipulating financial balances. [verified: Same as finding [8]: unrestricted workset.update(payload) with user JSON allowing override of role, approved, tier, and balance fields.]

Mass Assignment via unrestricted JSON merge into workset dictionary — Privilege escalation from viewer to admin role, unauthorized approval of actions, manipulation of financial balances, and corruption of business logic state. [verified: User-supplied JSON merged into workset dict via workset.update(payload) (line ~83) with no key filtering; attacker can override role, approved, tier, and balance fields.]

Hardcoded credentials (handle/verifier pairs) in partner console source code — Anyone with access to the source code (including via path traversal, source code leaks, or repository access) can extract the credential pairs and bypass the authentication check, gaining unauthorized access to the identity verification endpoint. [verified: Hardcoded verifier pairs {'north':'4812','south':'5930'} in source code (line ~112) serve as credential equivalents; source code exposure via path traversal or repo leak reveals them.]

CORS misconfiguration - arbitrary Origin reflection with credentials enabled — Any website on the internet can make authenticated cross-origin requests to the application, reading responses that include sensitive data. An attacker can host a malicious page that makes requests to the CRM API on behalf of authenticated users, exfiltrating their data including session tokens, PII, and business data. [verified: Same as finding [10]/[22]: permissive CORS with origin reflection and credentials enabled, allowing cross-origin data theft from any domain.]

Permissive CORS with reflected Origin and credentials enabled — Cross-origin data theft if the INTERNAL_OPS_TOKEN can be included in cross-origin requests, enabling attackers to read sensitive responses from the partner console endpoints. [verified: Origin header reflected verbatim into Access-Control-Allow-Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true (lines ~125-127); any origin can make credentialed cross-origin requests to this endpoint.]

Use of weak/insecure PRNG (random.choice) for token generation instead of secrets module — Security tokens generated with random.choice() are predictable. An attacker who observes multiple generated tokens can potentially predict future tokens, leading to token forgery and authentication bypass if these tokens are used for any security-sensitive purpose. [verified: Same as finding [9]/[24]: non-cryptographic random.choice() used for token generation; predictable PRNG output enables token forgery.]

SSL/TLS certificate verification explicitly disabled for HTTPS requests — Any data transmitted via this HTTPS connection can be intercepted and modified by a man-in-the-middle attacker. This could lead to data exfiltration, injection of malicious responses, and compromise of the integrity of communications with the partner endpoint. [verified: Same as finding [11]/[23]: ssl._create_unverified_context() disables TLS certificate validation, enabling MITM interception and tampering of outbound HTTPS traffic.]

Weak PRNG (random.choice) used for security token generation instead of secrets module — Predictable security tokens enabling forgery of nonces, session tokens, or other security-sensitive random values, depending on how the generated code is used downstream. [verified: Token generation uses random.choice() from the non-cryptographic random module (line ~160) instead of secrets module; Mersenne Twister output is predictable after observing enough values.]

Disabled TLS Certificate Verification in Partner Console — Man-in-the-middle attacks on outbound HTTPS connections, interception and modification of data sent to partner endpoints, credential theft. [verified: Same as finding [11]: ssl._create_unverified_context() disables TLS verification for outbound HTTPS, enabling MITM attacks.]

TLS certificate verification disabled for outbound HTTPS request — Machine-in-the-middle attacks intercepting or modifying data sent to external services [verified: Same as finding [11]/[23]/[39]: ssl._create_unverified_context() disables TLS verification on outbound HTTPS, enabling MITM interception of traffic.]

Use of cryptographically broken MD5 hash algorithm — MD5 is trivially broken and provides no meaningful security guarantees. If these digests were used for any security purpose (integrity verification, password hashing, or token generation), an attacker could easily forge collisions. Even as a non-security hash, its use indicates poor cryptographic hygiene. [verified: Same as finding [15]: hashlib.md5() is cryptographically broken; collisions are trivial and the hash provides no security guarantees for any downstream use.]

Use of Cryptographically Broken MD5 Hash Algorithm — Collision attacks and weakened hash integrity; if the MD5 output is used for any security purpose downstream (token generation, integrity checks, deduplication), it enables forgery and bypass. [verified: hashlib.md5() used for hashing user input (line ~100); MD5 is cryptographically broken and provides no collision or preimage resistance for any security-sensitive downstream use.]

Missing Authentication Gate on partner console endpoint acct_identity_ping_333 — Unauthenticated access to a partner console endpoint, violating the expected security boundary and potentially enabling reconnaissance or reflected data attacks. [verified: acct_identity_ping_333 (line ~103) does NOT call _wrk_gate() — it is the only partner console endpoint missing the token gate; unauthenticated access is possible, though impact is limited to echoing user input.]
